Main Points: • Structure: Establishes a bicameral legislature with the Senate and House of Representatives, where Senators are chosen by state legislatures for six-year terms while representatives are elected every two years. [1] • Eligibility & Representation: Mandates age requirements (25 in the House, 30 in the Senate) and residence within the state of election; mandates apportionment based on free persons and three-fifths of other inhabitants to ensure fair representation among states. [1] • Presidential Powers & Legislation: Requires bills from both chambers to be presented to the President for signing or vetoing; if the President returns a bill without objection within ten days (excluding Sundays), it becomes law unless Congress adjourns before its return, requiring a two-thirds vote in both houses. [2] • Commerce Clause & Orders: Grants Congress powers over national debt defense, uniform naturalization laws, coinage, and creation of federal tribunals; all orders requiring concurrence from both chambers must be approved by the President before taking effect. [2] • Supreme Court Jurisdiction: Establishes a single supreme court with appellate jurisdiction over ambassadors, maritime disputes, state-citizen controversies, and interstate/citizen cases. The trial of crimes (except impeachment) must be conducted by jury in the state where the crime occurred. [3] • Executive Leadership & Pardons: The President serves as Commander-in-Chief; holds the power to grant pardons for federal offenses and appoints judges and ambassadors with Senate approval. [3] • Constitutional Hierarchy & Treason: Establishes that the Constitution is the supreme law, superior to state laws, treaties under its authority, and defines treason as levying war against an enemy or aiding them; requires proof by two witnesses or a confession in open court for conviction.
